- **The PL/I Checkout Compiler** was built for the programmer's workbench. It translated code rapidly into an internal interpretive format, watching every step like a hawk to catch uninitialized variables, wild pointers, and out-of-bounds array subscripts with pinpoint English diagnostics.
- **The PL/I Optimizing Compiler** was built for the data center. Once a program was thoroughly debugged under the Checkout Compiler, engineers fed the exact same source code to the Optimizing Compiler, which took its time crafting streamlined, high-speed machine code for daily production runs.

questions.prompt: Why did IBM replace the original PL/I F compiler in 1971 with two separate products—the Checkout Compiler and the Optimizing Compiler?
choices: Rapid diagnostic debugging during development and maximum machine speed in production require opposite trade-offs.
One compiler was designed exclusively for scientific equations and the other exclusively for bank ledgers.
International software regulations taxed all-in-one compilers at twice the rate of paired software packages.
The Checkout Compiler only accepted paper tape input while the Optimizing Compiler only read punch cards.
questions.explanation: Developers testing new code need fast turnarounds and rich runtime error checking (Checkout), whereas finished production jobs need slow, thorough optimization for fast execution (Optimizing).

questions.prompt: How did a corporate programming team typically use the Checkout and Optimizing compilers together during a project?
choices: They ran both compilers simultaneously on two CPUs and kept whichever output finished first.
They used the Checkout Compiler to find and fix bugs quickly, then compiled the final code with the Optimizing Compiler.
They used the Optimizing Compiler to fix spelling mistakes and the Checkout Compiler to print customer invoices.
They compiled odd-numbered subroutines with Checkout and even-numbered subroutines with Optimizing.
questions.explanation: Teams developed and debugged code under the diagnostic-rich Checkout Compiler, then recompiled the verified source code with the Optimizing Compiler for fast production deployment.

chunks.title: Better Compilers, Persistent Fracture
chunks.content_markdown:
By the mid-1970s, the combination of Cornell's PL/C in classrooms and IBM's Checkout and Optimizing compilers in corporate data centers had largely solved the agonizing compile-time delays of 1966. On a roomy System/370 mainframe, the Optimizing Compiler generated brisk, reliable code that powered major banks and factories for decades.

Yet step back and look at what had happened to the dream of *one unified language*. To make PL/I workable in practice, IBM's own operating-system builders had retreated into in-house **PL/S**, universities relied on the **PL/C** subset, and commercial shops leased two separate expensive compilers just to cover development and production.

Meanwhile, hundreds of miles away in Cambridge, Massachusetts and Murray Hill, New Jersey, an even more dramatic test of PL/I had just played out—one where MIT, General Electric, and Bell Labs bet the world's most ambitious operating system on PL/I, and inadvertently sparked the birth of **Unix** and **C**.

questions.prompt: What pattern emerged across PL/S, Cornell PL/C, and the Checkout/Optimizing split by the early 1970s?
choices: Every user group had abandoned high-level programming and returned to wiring mechanical plugboards.
The original PL/I F compiler had proved so flawless that no new compilers were ever needed.
Making PL/I practical required splitting it into specialized dialects, subsets, and separate toolchains.
All three compilers were merged into a single 16-kilobyte program that ran on pocket calculators.
questions.explanation: Rather than one universal tool serving every need, practical adoption required specialized offshoots—PL/S for systems, PL/C for teaching, and a split Checkout/Optimizing pair for enterprise work.

questions.prompt: What improved significantly for enterprise PL/I users once IBM introduced the Optimizing Compiler on System/370 hardware?
choices: Programs no longer needed variables or semicolons and could be dictated by voice.
PL/I compilers became completely free and ran natively on every rival manufacturer's minicomputer.
Implicit type conversions and the I–N naming rule were permanently removed from the language.
Production machine-code speed and reliability matured, allowing large IBM shops to run heavy workloads efficiently.
questions.explanation: With larger System/370 memory and the Optimizing Compiler, PL/I's generated code quality improved dramatically, cementing its role in major IBM mainframe data centers.

sections.title: 7. The Multics Crucible: Betting an Operating System on High-Level PL/I (1965–1969)
sections.summary: Travel to Cambridge, Massachusetts, where MIT, General Electric, and AT&T Bell Labs launch Project Multics—an audacious effort to build a secure, multi-user time-sharing operating system almost entirely in PL/I rather than assembly language. While proving that high-level systems programming was possible, the project nearly collapsed under the weight of the contracted Early PL/I (EPL) compiler, whose huge, slow machine code helped drive Bell Labs to withdraw from Multics in 1969.
introduced_terms: Multics (Multiplexed Information and Computing Service)
high-level operating system implementation (replacing assembly kernels)
Early PL/I (EPL) compiler bottleneck (code bloat and compilation lag)

chunks.title: The Information Utility Dream
chunks.content_markdown:
In 1964, while most programmers still waited hours for batch punch-card printouts, researchers at **MIT**, **General Electric (GE)**, and **AT&T Bell Labs** joined forces to build a radical vision of interactive computing: **Multics** (*Multiplexed Information and Computing Service*).

Imagine computing delivered like electricity or telephone service. Instead of feeding card decks into a locked machine room, hundreds of engineers, scientists, and secretaries across a city would sit at interactive typewriter terminals connected over phone lines to a central GE-645 mainframe. Each user would feel as if they had the whole computer to themselves, complete with hierarchical file folders and hardware-enforced privacy.

Then the Multics architects made a decision that stunned the computing industry. Even though IBM's own engineers were struggling to write OS/360 in assembly language, MIT's Fernando Corbato and his partners decided to write almost the entire Multics operating system in brand-new **PL/I**.

questions.prompt: Which three institutional partners teamed up in the mid-1960s to build the Multics time-sharing system?
choices: IBM, Harvard University, and the U.S. Census Bureau.
MIT, General Electric (GE), and AT&T Bell Labs.
Cornell University, Digital Equipment Corporation, and Intel.
Stanford University, Burroughs Corporation, and NASA.
questions.explanation: Project Multics was a three-way consortium uniting MIT (Project MAC), General Electric (which supplied the GE-645 mainframe hardware), and AT&T Bell Labs.

questions.prompt: What everyday infrastructure model inspired the design of the Multics operating system?
choices: A municipal public utility, like electricity or phone service, serving many interactive terminal users at once.
A postal mail-order catalog where customers mailed punch cards in envelopes and waited two weeks.
A single-user pocket calculator that each engineer disconnected and carried home in a briefcase.
A television broadcast station that sent identical read-only spreadsheets to millions of screens.
questions.explanation: Multics was conceived as a continuous, reliable 'computing utility' that hundreds of people could access simultaneously from remote interactive terminals.

chunks.title: Daring to Replace Assembly Language
chunks.content_markdown:
Why was writing Multics in PL/I considered so audacious in 1965? At the time, conventional wisdom held that an operating system *had* to be written in low-level **assembly language**, where a human programmer hand-crafts every individual processor instruction. Hardware memory was scarce and expensive, and engineers believed no compiler could ever match the compactness and speed of hand-tuned assembly.

Yet assembly language had a crippling flaw: as operating systems grew to hundreds of thousands of lines, assembly code became a tangled, unreadable jungle where changing one data table broke fifty modules. By pioneering a **high-level operating system implementation**, the Multics leaders bet that a 5-line PL/I procedure could express what took 50 lines of cryptic assembly. With PL/I's nested data structures, pointers, character strings, and block structure, a small team of brilliant designers could inspect, modify, and secure the entire operating system rapidly.

questions.prompt: Why did almost all computer engineers in 1965 believe operating systems had to be written in assembly language?
choices: High-level languages were legally restricted to university classrooms by copyright treaties.
Assembly language was the only notation that could be typed on standard 80-column punch cards.
Engineers believed only hand-crafted assembly instructions could run fast and compactly enough for a kernel.
Compilers had not yet been invented for any scientific or commercial programming language.
questions.explanation: Because early mainframes had tight memory and slow processors, conventional wisdom insisted that operating systems required the tight, manual instruction control of assembly language.

questions.prompt: What major advantage did the Multics architects hope to gain by writing their operating system in high-level PL/I instead of assembly?
choices: They could run the GE-645 mainframe without connecting it to an electrical power outlet.
They could eliminate the need for magnetic disk drives and store all files on paper tape.
They could prevent users from ever creating sub-directories or passwords on their accounts.
They could express complex kernel logic in far fewer, clearer lines of code that were much easier to maintain.
questions.explanation: A high-level language like PL/I allowed complex data structures and control flow to be written concisely and clearly, making a large operating system far easier to understand, debug, and evolve.

chunks.title: The Early PL/I (EPL) Compiler Bottleneck
chunks.content_markdown:
Bold visions soon met a harsh practical hurdle: in 1965, General Electric's GE-645 mainframe had *no PL/I compiler*. When an outside software firm contracted to build the compiler missed its deadline and collapsed, the Multics team faced disaster—they had hundreds of pages of operating system designs written in PL/I and no way to run them.

In a heroic emergency sprint, Bell Labs wizards Douglas McIlroy and Robert Morris—joined by MIT researchers—built a working subset compiler called **EPL** (**Early PL/I**).

EPL saved the project from immediate cancellation, but it created the **Early PL/I (EPL) compiler bottleneck**. Because full PL/I allowed dynamic string lengths, complex pointer offsets, and recursive stack frames at any moment, EPL frequently had to emit slow library calls and conservative machine instructions just in case. Compiling a single kernel module took agonizing minutes, and the resulting binary files were huge—often five to ten times larger than anyone had budgeted.

questions.prompt: Why did Bell Labs researchers Douglas McIlroy and Robert Morris have to hurriedly build the Early PL/I (EPL) compiler?
choices: IBM refused to sell System/360 mainframes to universities located in Massachusetts.
An outside contractor hired to build the GE-645 PL/I compiler failed to deliver a working product.
The original Multics source code was accidentally destroyed in a laboratory fire in 1966.
General Electric changed the GE-645 from a binary computer to a ternary computer mid-project.
questions.explanation: When the commercial vendor contracted to write the GE-645 PL/I compiler failed to deliver, Bell Labs and MIT engineers had to build EPL themselves to keep Multics alive.

questions.prompt: How did the complexity of PL/I's language rules contribute to the Early PL/I (EPL) compiler bottleneck?
choices: To support general-purpose strings, pointers, and dynamic frames, EPL generated huge, slow machine code.
EPL could only translate one letter per second because it had to consult a dictionary on punch cards.
PL/I required the GE-645 to reboot its magnetic core memory after every single subroutine call.
EPL refused to compile any operating system module that contained more than three variables.
questions.explanation: Because PL/I's semantics allowed very general dynamic behavior (like varying strings and complex argument descriptors), the rushed EPL compiler generated bloated, slow object code.

chunks.title: Thrashing Drums and the Fight to Tame PL/I
chunks.content_markdown:
What happens when an operating system made of giant, bloated PL/I modules tries to run inside limited 1967 main memory? Every time a user typed a simple command at a terminal, Multics had to swap dozens of oversized code pages in and out from spinning magnetic drums. The system spent almost $$100\%$$ of its time shuffling memory pages back and forth—a paralysis computer scientists named **thrashing**.

Critics gleefully declared that writing an operating system in PL/I was a proven failure. Yet MIT's team refused to surrender. Analyzing their own code, they discovered that programmers were casually using expensive PL/I features—like general-purpose `ON`-units and arbitrary-length bit strings—inside tiny inner loops where a simple integer would do.

By educating programmers on which PL/I constructs were cheap vs. costly, and by engineering a brand-new, highly optimizing GE/Honeywell PL/I compiler, the team shrank kernel modules by factors of five and sped them up tenfold.

questions.prompt: Why did the oversized machine code produced by the EPL compiler cause early versions of Multics to suffer from 'thrashing'?
choices: The cooling fans vibrated violently whenever the processor executed fixed-point decimal division.
The typewriter terminals struck their paper ribbons so rapidly that the mechanical typebars jammed.
Bloated kernel modules overflowed main memory, forcing constant, crippling page swaps to and from magnetic drums.
Multiple users editing the same file caused the magnetic tape reels to spin in opposite directions.
questions.explanation: Because EPL-compiled procedures were so large, they did not fit comfortably in core memory, causing the virtual-memory system to spend all its time swapping pages ('thrashing') instead of doing useful work.

questions.prompt: How did the MIT and GE/Honeywell teams ultimately rescue Multics's performance without abandoning PL/I?
choices: They replaced all user terminals with batch punch-card readers so only one person could log in per day.
They rewrote ninety percent of the operating system in COBOL and ran it on an IBM 1401.
They outlawed subroutines entirely and placed the entire operating system inside a single five-line loop.
They trained coders to avoid high-overhead PL/I constructs and built a vastly better optimizing PL/I compiler.
questions.explanation: By sticking to a disciplined subset of low-overhead PL/I constructs and building a sophisticated production PL/I compiler, the team made Multics fast, compact, and commercially viable.

chunks.title: Vindication at MIT, Exhaustion at Bell Labs
chunks.content_markdown:
In the long run, Multics was a triumph. Running on Honeywell mainframes through the 1970s and 1980s (with its last machine shutting down only in the year 2000), it pioneered tree-structured file folders, connecting code modules on the fly (*dynamic linking*), concentric hardware privilege layers (*ring-based security*), and proved beyond doubt that complex operating systems *should* be written in high-level languages.

Yet that turnaround came too late to save the original three-way alliance. By early 1969, executives at **AT&T Bell Labs** had grown exhausted with the delays, the millions of dollars spent, and the sheer weight of Multics and its EPL toolchain. In April 1969, Bell Labs pulled out of the project.

Back in Murray Hill, New Jersey, two young Bell Labs researchers named **Ken Thompson** and **Dennis Ritchie** suddenly lost access to their interactive Multics environment. Disillusioned by the mammoth complexity of both Multics and PL/I, they set out on a spare minicomputer to prove that systems software could be built the exact opposite way.

questions.prompt: What lasting historical milestone did Project Multics achieve despite its painful early compiler struggles?
choices: It proved that a large, secure, full-featured operating system could be successfully written in a high-level language.
It convinced every computer manufacturer in the world to standardize on the 36-bit GE-645 processor.
It demonstrated that assembly language was always superior to compiled languages for file management.
It eliminated the need for computer passwords by physically locking every terminal in a bank vault.
questions.explanation: Multics validated high-level systems programming and introduced foundational OS concepts (hierarchical file systems, dynamic linking, security rings) that shaped all modern operating systems.

questions.prompt: What pivotal decision did AT&T Bell Labs make in April 1969 after years of frustration with Multics's delays and complexity?
choices: Bell Labs purchased General Electric's computer division and mandated PL/I across the telephone network.
Bell Labs withdrew from the Multics consortium, leaving researchers like Thompson and Ritchie to seek a simpler path.
Bell Labs moved its entire research staff to Hursley, England to help IBM maintain the PL/I F compiler.
Bell Labs outlawed time-sharing terminals and required all scientists to use mechanical slide rules.
questions.explanation: Concluding that Multics was too slow, complex, and expensive for its immediate needs, Bell Labs withdrew in 1969—setting the stage for Thompson and Ritchie to create Unix and C.

sections.title: 8. The Unix and C Counter-Revolution: Bell Labs Embraces Radical Simplicity
sections.summary: Follow Bell Labs researchers Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie as they retreat from the sprawling complexity of Multics and PL/I to a modest DEC minicomputer, forging the minimalist Unix operating system. After Thompson briefly experimented with miniature compiler tools, they pivoted through BCPL and B to create C—a compact, portable systems language that kept PL/I's curly-style block structure and slash-star comments while stripping away hidden runtime machinery so every statement mapped transparently to hardware instructions.
introduced_terms: post-Multics simplicity backlash (Unix minimalist philosophy)
transparent hardware mapping (zero hidden runtime overhead)
BCPL-to-B-to-C systems lineage (portable minicomputer alternative)

chunks.title: From a Mainframe Palace to a Cupboard Minicomputer
chunks.content_markdown:
When AT&T Bell Labs pulled out of Project Multics in April 1969, researchers **Ken Thompson** and **Dennis Ritchie** went from working on a multimillion-dollar mainframe utility to scavenging an idle DEC PDP-7 **minicomputer** sitting in a corner at Murray Hill, New Jersey. Compared to the giant GE-645, the PDP-7 was tiny—possessing just $$8,192$$ 18-bit words of memory—yet Thompson and Ritchie realized that its smallness was actually a liberation.

Instead of writing a thousand-page specification for a system that tried to do everything for everyone, they built a lean, nimble operating system around a handful of simple, composable tools. Even the name they adopted—**Unix** (originally spelled *Unics*, short for *Uniplexed* Information and Computing Service)—was a pointed pun on *Multics*: where Multics was a sprawling, multi-layered monolith, Unix would do one thing at a time and do it well.

questions.prompt: What inside joke was embedded in the original name 'Unics' (Unix) chosen by Bell Labs researchers in 1969?
choices: It stood for 'Universal Numeric IBM Compiler System' to honor the Hursley laboratory.
It contrasted 'Uniplexed' (doing one thing simply) against 'Multiplexed' in the sprawling Multics project.
It indicated that the operating system could only be used by university freshmen during their first week.
It meant the computer used only the number one and outlawed the binary digit zero.
questions.explanation: 'Unics' (later Unix) was a playful contrast to 'Multics'—celebrating a small, single-minded, minimalist system over a massive, over-engineered monolith.

questions.prompt: How did the hardware environment where Unix was born differ from the GE-645 mainframe used by Multics?
choices: Unix began on a modest, memory-constrained DEC minicomputer rather than a multimillion-dollar mainframe.
Unix was built on an analog mechanical differential analyzer driven by brass gears.
Unix ran on a network of five hundred IBM System/360 mainframes linked by satellite.
Unix required no electronic memory at all because it executed directly from punch cards.
questions.explanation: Thompson began building Unix on a scavenged DEC PDP-7 minicomputer with tiny memory, forcing every design choice to be radically simple and compact.

chunks.title: The Creed of Transparent Hardware Mapping
chunks.content_markdown:
Scarred by their years wrestling with Multics's Early PL/I (EPL) compiler, Thompson and Ritchie led what historians call the **post-Multics simplicity backlash**. They asked a penetrating question: why had PL/I caused so much grief when used to write operating system code?

The problem was that PL/I hid enormous machinery behind innocent-looking syntax. In PL/I, writing a simple line to copy a string or add two variables might secretly call a hundred-line runtime routine to convert decimal scales, check dynamic string lengths, or set up `ON`-condition error frames. The programmer could not *see* the cost of their code.

In response, the Bell Labs team demanded **transparent hardware mapping**: in a true systems language, every statement you write should map directly and predictably to a few machine instructions, with **zero hidden runtime overhead**. If a program needed memory allocation or formatted printing, that belonged in an optional library function you called explicitly—never wired silently into the grammar.

questions.prompt: What core lesson did Thompson and Ritchie draw from their frustrating experience with PL/I on the Multics project?
choices: High-level languages should never allow subroutines to take parameters or return values.
Operating systems should only be used in batch mode with 80-column paper punch cards.
A systems language must avoid hidden runtime machinery so programmers can see the exact hardware cost of every line.
Compilers should automatically convert all integers into character strings before storing them on disk.
questions.explanation: Having seen PL/I hide expensive conversions, descriptors, and runtime calls behind simple statements, Thompson and Ritchie prized transparent, predictable mapping to machine instructions.

questions.prompt: How does a language with 'transparent hardware mapping' handle features like formatted input/output (`printf`) compared to PL/I?
choices: It bans printing altogether and requires users to read binary lights on the front panel.
It builds fifty different printing keywords directly into the compiler's core grammar.
It requires a human operator to translate binary output into English on a separate typewriter.
It keeps input/output out of the core grammar and provides it through explicit, optional library functions.
questions.explanation: Whereas PL/I baked `GET`/`PUT` and `READ`/`WRITE` into the language grammar itself, C removed all I/O from the compiler and placed it in standard library functions like `printf`.

chunks.title: From BCPL to B to C
chunks.content_markdown:
Ironically, when Ken Thompson first wanted a high-level language for the tiny PDP-7 in 1969, his very first instinct was to write a miniature subset of PL/I! Within days, however, he realized that even a stripped-down PL/I carried too many data-type rules to fit inside the PDP-7's tiny memory.

Instead, Thompson turned to **BCPL**, a clean, typeless systems language designed by Martin Richards at Cambridge University that had also been used at MIT. Thompson pared BCPL's syntax down to the bone—removing every non-essential word so the entire compiler fit in just a few kilobytes—and named the resulting language **B**.

When Bell Labs acquired a newer 16-bit DEC **PDP-11** minicomputer in 1970, B hit a snag: B treated all memory as uniform machine words, whereas the PDP-11 addressed individual 8-bit character bytes. Between 1971 and 1973, **Dennis Ritchie** added lightweight hardware data types (`char` for bytes, `int` for words, `struct` for records) to B—completing the **BCPL-to-B-to-C systems lineage** and creating **C**.

questions.prompt: Why did Ken Thompson abandon his initial 1969 attempt to write a small PL/I subset compiler for the PDP-7 minicomputer?
choices: IBM threatened legal action if the letters 'PL' appeared on a Digital Equipment Corporation minicomputer.
Even a trimmed PL/I subset was too bulky for the PDP-7's tiny memory, so he stripped down BCPL into B instead.
The PDP-7 processor could only execute decimal COBOL instructions and lacked binary addition circuits.
Bell Labs management required all experimental compilers to be compatible with Cambridge University's BCPL.
questions.explanation: Realizing that PL/I's type and runtime model was too heavy for a tiny minicomputer, Thompson instead simplified Martin Richards's BCPL into the ultra-compact language B.

questions.prompt: What hardware feature of the new 16-bit DEC PDP-11 minicomputer prompted Dennis Ritchie to evolve the typeless B language into C?
choices: The PDP-11 addressed individual 8-bit bytes as well as 16-bit words, requiring distinct character and integer types.
The PDP-11 used base-10 decimal registers that could only be programmed with fixed-point scale factors.
The PDP-11 had megabytes of core memory, allowing Ritchie to restore all of PL/I's automatic conversion tables.
The PDP-11 lacked hardware index registers and required all arrays to be stored on magnetic tape.
questions.explanation: Because the PDP-11 was byte-addressable, B's single word-oriented cell type was awkward; Ritchie added hardware-matched types (`char`, `int`, pointers, and `struct`) to create C.

chunks.title: The PL/I Features Hiding Inside C
chunks.content_markdown:
Although C was born as a minimalist rebellion against PL/I, take a close look at a page of C code and you will spot a surprising family resemblance. Thompson and Ritchie had spent four years immersed in PL/I on Multics, and they happily kept the parts of PL/I that didn't bloat the compiler!

Where did C get its familiar `/* ... */` block comment delimiters? Straight from PL/I. Where did C get the distinction between `auto` (stack variables created when a function starts) and `static` (variables that keep their value across calls), as well as `extern` declarations across files? Directly from PL/I's `AUTOMATIC`, `STATIC`, and `EXTERNAL` storage classes. Even C's `struct` records and heavy reliance on typed memory **pointers** were streamlined descendants of PL/I's structures and pointer variables.

In short, C did not reject high-level structure; it kept PL/I's clean structural skeleton while throwing away its giant conversion matrix, fixed-point decimal traps, and built-in I/O.

questions.prompt: Which familiar syntactic and storage concepts did Dennis Ritchie's C language inherit directly from PL/I?
choices: Fixed-point decimal division precision rules and the implicit I–N variable naming default.
Built-in PICTURE currency formatting and automatic syntax error repair during batch compilation.
Slash-star block comments, auto/static/extern storage lifetimes, structured records, and typed pointers.
English-like arithmetic sentences and mandatory sequence numbers in columns 73 through 80.
questions.explanation: Having programmed extensively in PL/I on Multics, Thompson and Ritchie carried over PL/I's `/* */` comments, `auto`/`static`/`extern` storage classes, structured records, and pointers into C.

questions.prompt: How can C's design philosophy best be summarized in relation to PL/I?
choices: C doubled the size of PL/I's grammar so it could also run COBOL payroll decks without modification.
C abolished pointers, structures, and subroutines, returning programmers to line-numbered BASIC.
C kept PL/I's automatic bit-string coercions while removing block structure and local variables.
C retained PL/I's block-structured, pointer-friendly skeleton while stripping away hidden runtime overhead.
questions.explanation: C preserved the expressive power of structured blocks, data structures, and pointers while eliminating everything that required a massive compiler or hidden runtime library.

chunks.title: Why Unix and C Swept the 1970s
chunks.content_markdown:
In 1973, Thompson and Ritchie rewrote the Unix kernel in C. Think about that milestone: the dream that MIT and Bell Labs had struggled for years to achieve on a giant mainframe with Multics and PL/I—an operating system written in a portable high-level language—was now running briskly in C on a modest minicomputer!

Because the C compiler was small, fast, and easy to retarget to a new processor in a few weeks, Unix and C became the first truly **portable** systems ecosystem. Universities, which could obtain Unix source code from AT&T for a nominal tape fee, taught an entire generation of computer science students to think in C.

While PL/I remained tethered to expensive mainframes, C rode the minicomputer wave across the world. Yet an even smaller hardware revolution was simultaneously brewing in California—where another computer scientist was asking whether a slimmed-down child of PL/I could power the brand-new **microprocessor**.

questions.prompt: What historic milestone did Thompson and Ritchie achieve in 1973 that fulfilled the original high-level systems dream of Multics?
choices: They rewrote the Unix operating system kernel in C, making the OS portable across different computers.
They compiled the entire IBM OS/360 operating system inside a 4-kilobyte pocket calculator.
They convinced the ANSI committee to rename the C language 'PL/II' across all government contracts.
They eliminated the need for a compiler by building a minicomputer that executed English sentences directly.
questions.explanation: Rewriting the Unix kernel in C in 1973 proved that a lean high-level language could deliver both low-level efficiency and cross-platform operating system portability.

questions.prompt: Why was C able to spread across different manufacturers' computers in the 1970s so much faster than full PL/I?
choices: Federal law required every minicomputer buyer to delete all non-C compilers upon delivery.
C's compiler was small and simple enough that one or two engineers could port it to a new CPU in weeks.
C programs did not need to be compiled at all because every CPU used the exact same binary code.
IBM paid universities millions of dollars in grants to replace their System/370 mainframes with PDP-11s.
questions.explanation: Because C had a compact grammar and minimal runtime requirements, retargeting the C compiler to a new processor architecture required only a small fraction of the effort needed to build a full PL/I compiler.

sections.title: 9. Shrinking for the Microprocessor Dawn: Gary Kildall's PL/M and the PC Era
sections.summary: Trace PL/I's surprising second life at the birth of the personal computer revolution, when computer scientist Gary Kildall designed PL/M (Programming Language for Microcomputers) in 1973 for Intel's 8-bit 8008 and 8080 chips and used it to write the landmark CP/M operating system. We then explore why full-scale PL/I—even after the streamlined ANSI Subset G and Digital Research's PL/I-80 arrived—proved too heavy and mainframe-bound to capture the 1980s PC, Unix workstation, and 1990s web waves.
introduced_terms: PL/M (Programming Language for Microcomputers)
CP/M (Control Program for Microcomputers)
ANSI PL/I Subset G and PL/I-80 (microcomputer slimmed standard)

chunks.title: A Mainframe Language Meets a Fingernail Chip
chunks.content_markdown:
In 1972, while C was taking shape at Bell Labs, a computer science professor at the Naval Postgraduate School in Monterey, California named **Gary Kildall** visited a young Silicon Valley chipmaker called **Intel**. Intel had recently created the first single-chip **microprocessors**—the 4-bit 4004 and the 8-bit 8008, soon followed by the famed **Intel 8080**. For the first time in history, an entire central processing unit fit onto a sliver of silicon the size of a fingernail.

Early hardware engineers assumed that a tiny 8-bit microchip with only $$4\text{ to }16\text{ kilobytes}$$ of memory could only be programmed by toggling binary switches or writing painstaking assembly language. Kildall, who had written compilers and admired the clean block structure of mainframe PL/I, saw a much bigger opportunity. What if you distilled PL/I down to its leanest structural essence so engineers could write microchip software in a readable, high-level language?

questions.prompt: What hardware breakthrough at Intel in the early 1970s inspired Gary Kildall to rethink how small computers were programmed?
choices: The invention of the 80-column rectangular-hole paper punch card.
The introduction of 64-kilobyte magnetic core memory cabinets for railroad billing.
The creation of single-chip 8-bit microprocessors like the Intel 8008 and 8080.
The deployment of transatlantic fiber-optic cables for banking mainframes.
questions.explanation: Intel's 8008 and 8080 microprocessors placed an entire 8-bit CPU on a single silicon chip, opening the door to inexpensive microcomputers.

questions.prompt: What conventional assumption about early 8-bit microprocessors did Gary Kildall challenge?
choices: That microprocessors were too small for high-level languages and had to be programmed in raw assembly or binary.
That microprocessors could only run inside orbiting spacecraft where zero gravity cooled the silicon.
That microprocessors could execute full mainframe COBOL compilers without any modifications.
That microprocessors required three full-time human operators to oil their mechanical gears.
questions.explanation: Hardware engineers assumed tiny microchips could only be programmed in assembly language; Kildall showed that a streamlined, PL/I-style high-level language could target them efficiently.

chunks.title: PL/M: PL/I Tailored for 8-Bit Silicon
chunks.content_markdown:
In 1973, working as a consultant for Intel, Gary Kildall unveiled **PL/M** (*Programming Language for Microcomputers*)—the first high-level programming language ever built for microprocessors.

Anyone who had written PL/I recognized PL/M at a glance. It used `DECLARE` statements, `DO ... END` blocks, `IF ... THEN ... ELSE` branches, and `/* ... */` comments. Yet to make the output razor-sharp for an 8-bit Intel chip, Kildall stripped away every trace of mainframe bloat. PL/M had no floating-point decimals, no bit-string coercions, and no hidden runtime library. Instead, it offered just two hardware-native data types:

- **`BYTE`**: an 8-bit unsigned whole number ($$0$$ to $$255$$), matching a single 8080 register.
- **`ADDRESS`**: a 16-bit memory pointer ($$0$$ to $$65,535$$), matching the chip's $$64\text{-kilobyte}$$ memory address bus.

Like IBM's in-house PL/S and Bell Labs' C, every line of PL/M compiled directly into tight, predictable machine instructions.

questions.prompt: How did Gary Kildall's PL/M language adapt PL/I's design to fit the 8-bit Intel 8008 and 8080 microprocessors?
choices: It kept PL/I's block syntax but restricted data types to hardware-native 8-bit BYTE and 16-bit ADDRESS values.
It doubled the precision of fixed-point decimal division from fifteen digits to thirty digits in hardware.
It required every microcomputer to connect over a modem to an IBM System/370 mainframe at runtime.
It replaced all English keywords with two-digit hexadecimal numbers to conserve floppy disk sectors.
questions.explanation: PL/M preserved PL/I's readable structured syntax while replacing mainframe data types and runtime libraries with direct 8-bit (`BYTE`) and 16-bit (`ADDRESS`) hardware primitives.

questions.prompt: What similarity did Kildall's PL/M share with both IBM's in-house PL/S and Dennis Ritchie's C?
choices: All three languages were withheld from universities and outside customers until the late 1990s.
All three languages eliminated PL/I's heavy runtime overhead so code mapped transparently to hardware.
All three languages used the exact same multi-pass disk overlay architecture written at Hursley.
All three languages were designed exclusively for calculating actuarial life-insurance tables.
questions.explanation: In three different computing worlds—IBM mainframes (PL/S), DEC minicomputers (C), and Intel microprocessors (PL/M)—engineers independently stripped away PL/I's runtime bloat to achieve transparent systems programming.

chunks.title: How PL/M Built CP/M and Kickstarted the PC Era
chunks.content_markdown:
In 1974, Gary Kildall used his new PL/M language to write a compact operating system that allowed an Intel 8080 microcomputer to load programs and store files on an 8-inch floppy disk. He called it **CP/M** (*Control Program for Microcomputers*) and founded **Digital Research** to sell it.

Because the core of CP/M was written in high-level PL/M rather than tangled assembly code, adapting CP/M to run on dozens of different early personal computers took only a small hardware-interface tweak. Throughout the late 1970s, CP/M became the industry-standard operating system of the early personal computer revolution—and its command prompt (`A>`), `DIR` listings, and three-letter filename extensions (`.COM`, `.TXT`) became the direct blueprint for **MS-DOS** on the 1981 IBM PC.

Thus, through PL/M and CP/M, a streamlined descendant of PL/I quietly midwifed the personal computer software industry!

questions.prompt: What landmark early personal computer operating system did Gary Kildall write in PL/M in 1974?
choices: OS/360, which managed batch job queues on room-sized magnetic-core mainframes.
Multics, which served hundreds of dial-up typewriter terminals from Cambridge.
RSTS/E, which ran time-shared interactive BASIC on 16-bit DEC minicomputers.
CP/M, which became the standard floppy-disk operating system of late-1970s microcomputers.
questions.explanation: Kildall wrote CP/M (Control Program for Microcomputers) in PL/M to manage floppy-disk files on Intel 8080 machines, creating the standard operating system of the pre-IBM-PC era.

questions.prompt: How did CP/M leave a visible mark on the 1980s IBM PC and Microsoft MS-DOS experience?
choices: Its drive-letter prompts, DIR command, and three-letter file extensions served as the direct model for MS-DOS.
It required all early IBM PC users to submit spreadsheet formulas on 80-column paper punch cards.
It forced Microsoft Windows to use PL/I's fixed-point division rules for all desktop screen coordinates.
It standardized the use of magnetic core memory rings inside portable laptop computers.
questions.explanation: Early MS-DOS (originally 86-DOS/QDOS) was closely modeled on CP/M's user interface and disk conventions so existing CP/M software could be ported easily.

chunks.title: Subset G and PL/I-80: Full PL/I Tries to Fit on a Desk
chunks.content_markdown:
If PL/M succeeded as a bare-metal microchip tool, could *real* application-level PL/I also make the leap onto desktop personal computers? By the late 1970s, standards committees had finally learned the lesson of PL/I's early bloat. In 1981, ANSI approved a clean, disciplined standard called **ANSI PL/I Subset G** (*General-Purpose Subset*), which kept PL/I's best structured programming, string, decimal, and file features while pruning away its obscure redundancies and wildest conversion traps.

Gary Kildall jumped at the chance to bring his favorite mainframe language to desktop machines. In 1980, Digital Research released **PL/I-80**, a remarkable Subset G compiler that ran inside just $$48\text{ kilobytes}$$ on an 8-bit CP/M computer (followed later by **PL/I-86** for the IBM PC). Ironically, Kildall had proven on a tiny desktop floppy disk what Hursley had struggled to do on a room-sized System/360 in 1966: a fast, clean PL/I compiler inside less than $$64\text{ kilobytes}$$!

questions.prompt: What was the goal of the 'ANSI PL/I Subset G' standard developed in the late 1970s and early 1980s?
choices: To restrict PL/I exclusively to graphics supercomputers owned by Hollywood film studios.
To double the number of keywords in PL/I by merging it with Ada and LISP.
To define a clean, practical general-purpose PL/I without the obscure redundancies and traps of full PL/I.
To remove all decimal arithmetic and character strings so PL/I looked identical to 1957 FORTRAN.
questions.explanation: ANSI Subset G ('General-Purpose Subset') trimmed full PL/I into a cohesive, orthogonal language small enough for minicomputers and microcomputers while keeping its core strengths.

questions.prompt: What historical irony did Gary Kildall's Digital Research achieve with its PL/I-80 compiler in 1980?
choices: It sold the compiler exclusively to IBM to replace Hursley's Optimizing Compiler on mainframes.
It fit a fast, working Subset G PL/I compiler onto an 8-bit desktop microcomputer with under 64 KB of RAM.
It required users to mail their floppy disks to England for compilation and wait two weeks.
It proved that PL/I could only run on processors built out of mechanical relays.
questions.explanation: Fourteen years after Hursley agonized over fitting PL/I F into 64 KB on a room-sized mainframe, Kildall's team fit a brisk Subset G compiler (PL/I-80) into 48–64 KB on a desktop microcomputer.

chunks.title: Why Full PL/I Missed the PC, Workstation, and Web Waves
chunks.content_markdown:
Even with Subset G and Kildall's impressive PL/I-80 compiler, PL/I never became the lingua franca of the 1980s personal computer boom, the Unix engineering workstation era, or the 1990s internet revolution. Why did it miss those waves?

First, **culture and price**: when an amateur or startup bought an Apple II or an IBM PC, Microsoft **BASIC** came free in the box, and Borland's **Turbo Pascal** cost just $$\$49.95$$ with an instant built-in screen editor. Commercial PL/I compilers remained relatively expensive, multi-pass command-line tools aimed at corporate mainframe veterans.

Second, **the Unix and C tidal wave**: by the mid-1980s, university computer science departments were graduating thousands of engineers fluent in C. When those graduates built the graphical interfaces of the Macintosh and Windows, the networking protocols of the Internet, and new languages like C++, Java, Python, and JavaScript, they naturally built on the C ecosystem—leaving PL/I behind inside corporate mainframe data centers.

questions.prompt: Why did languages like BASIC, Turbo Pascal, and C outpace PL/I-80 among 1980s personal computer developers?
choices: PL/I-80 was banned by the Federal Communications Commission from running on home electrical wiring.
BASIC and Turbo Pascal could calculate twenty-digit decimal fractions, whereas PL/I only supported integers.
Personal computer keyboards lacked the semicolon and slash keys required to type PL/I statements.
They were cheaper or bundled free, offered instant interactive workflows, and had massive university and hobbyist momentum.
questions.explanation: Bundled BASIC, inexpensive and ultra-fast IDEs like Turbo Pascal, and the university-backed rise of C captured the microcomputer developer mindshare before desktop PL/I could gain traction.

questions.prompt: How did university computer science education in the 1980s shape the software ecosystems of the 1990s web era?
choices: Graduates trained on Unix and C naturally built new operating systems, networks, and languages in the C tradition.
Universities outlawed all compiled languages in 1982 and taught only punch-card plugboard wiring.
Every computer science major was required to sign a pledge never to use block comments or pointers.
Academic departments standardized exclusively on IBM PL/S after IBM released it into the public domain.
questions.explanation: Because universities widely adopted Unix and C, a generation of graduates carried C's syntax and tooling into workstations, PCs, the Internet, and successor languages like C++, Java, and JavaScript.

sections.title: 10. Mainframe Twilight and Enduring DNA: How PL/I Secretly Shaped Modern Code
sections.summary: Conclude our two-part journey by examining the paradox of PL/I today: a language rarely taught in universities that still processes trillions of dollars in mission-critical mainframe banking, insurance, and airline reservation vaults. Even more remarkably, we trace how almost every bold idea PL/I pioneered in 1964—from slash-star block comments, typed pointers, and VARYING length-prefixed strings to native decimal math, array slicing, and ON-condition exception handling—was quietly absorbed into C, SQL, Ada, Java, Python, and C#.
introduced_terms: mission-critical mainframe persistence (legacy transaction processing)
VARYING string and native decimal inheritance (SQL VARCHAR and DECIMAL)
PL/I architectural DNA (pointers, slash-star comments, and exception handling)

chunks.title: The Invisible Engine Behind Your Bank Card
chunks.content_markdown:
Open any modern survey of the most popular programming languages in Silicon Valley or university classrooms—Python, JavaScript, Java, C++, C#, Go, Rust—and you will have to scroll a very long way to find **PL/I**. To a casual observer, IBM's 1964 universal contender looks like an extinct dinosaur from the punch-card era.

Yet if you could wave a wand and pause every running PL/I program on Earth for ten minutes tomorrow morning, global commerce would convulse. ATM networks across Europe and North America would reject withdrawals, major logistics and auto-manufacturing pipelines would stall, government tax and pension clearinghouses would freeze, and trillions of dollars in insurance and banking settlements would halt.

How can a language that almost no college student learns today still quietly process a vast share of the planet's most sensitive financial and industrial transactions?

questions.prompt: What striking paradox characterizes the status of the PL/I programming language in the 21st century?
choices: It is the most popular language for mobile phone games, yet no bank or insurer has ever used it.
It is rarely taught in universities today, yet it still powers trillions of dollars in core mainframe transactions.
It can only be executed on 1960s magnetic-core hardware, yet every new laptop ships with a PL/I key.
It was outlawed by international banking treaties in 1999, yet hobbyists still punch it onto paper tape.
questions.explanation: Although PL/I vanished from mainstream academic and startup culture, it remains deeply embedded in mission-critical mainframe banking, insurance, manufacturing, and government systems.

questions.prompt: Where are the majority of active production PL/I programs executing in the modern computing landscape?
choices: Inside wearable fitness trackers and smart household thermostats.
Inside browser-based social media animations running on smartphones.
Inside core transaction systems at major banks, insurers, manufacturers, and government agencies.
Inside amateur radio telegraphy repeaters operating on shortwave frequencies.
questions.explanation: Large financial, insurance, industrial, and government institutions that standardized on IBM mainframes in the 1960s–1980s continue to run massive production workloads in PL/I.

chunks.title: Why Mission-Critical Mainframe Code Persists
chunks.content_markdown:
Economists and software historians call this phenomenon **mission-critical mainframe persistence**. Over forty or fifty years, a major bank or insurance carrier may have invested tens of thousands of programmer-years refining a 15-million-line PL/I system running on IBM System/370 descendants—today's **IBM zSystems** mainframes.

Every obscure regulatory rule, currency rounding corner case, and high-speed database lock has been battle-tested through decades of real-world storms. Attempting to rewrite all 15 million lines from scratch in a newer language costs hundreds of millions of dollars and carries a terrifying risk of introducing subtle bugs that miscalculate customer accounts.

Instead, enterprises modernize in place. IBM actively develops **Enterprise PL/I for z/OS** today—adding 64-bit addressing, Unicode text, XML and **JSON** parsers, and seamless web APIs so a rock-solid 1978 PL/I banking core can answer a customer's smartphone tap in a few milliseconds.

questions.prompt: Why do major banks and insurers often keep battle-tested PL/I mainframe systems running rather than rewriting them from scratch?
choices: Modern programming languages like Java and Python are mathematically incapable of adding dollars and cents.
IBM mainframes weld their magnetic disk drives shut so existing software can never be deleted.
Rewriting millions of lines of debugged business logic carries massive cost and high risk of new subtle bugs.
International copyright law forbids translating any program written before 1980 into a newer language.
questions.explanation: Decades-old transaction systems encode vast, thoroughly debugged business and regulatory logic; replacing them wholesale is extraordinarily expensive and risky compared to maintaining and wrapping them.

questions.prompt: How do modern IBM zSystems mainframes allow legacy PL/I applications to work alongside smartphone apps and web services?
choices: Human clerks read the mainframe's paper printouts and type the numbers into smartphones by hand.
Smartphones must plug into an 80-column card reader via a special USB adapter cable.
The mainframe converts all web traffic into 5-unit Baudot telegraph code before PL/I reads it.
Updated Enterprise PL/I compilers support 64-bit memory, Unicode, JSON/XML parsing, and modern network APIs.
questions.explanation: IBM continuously updates Enterprise PL/I for z/OS with native support for JSON, XML, Unicode, and web service interfaces so core PL/I logic can serve modern digital front ends.

chunks.title: How PL/I Shaped SQL Databases and Business Types
chunks.content_markdown:
Even if you never touch an IBM mainframe, you interact with PL/I's inventions every single day—because modern languages quietly raided PL/I's treasure chest of ideas! Start with **VARYING string and native decimal inheritance**.

Before 1964, FORTRAN and COBOL forced strings into rigid, fixed-length boxes padded with spaces. PL/I pioneered `CHARACTER(n) VARYING`: a text string that prefixed its characters with a hidden length counter so names and sentences could grow, shrink, and concatenate naturally. When IBM researchers Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce designed the **SQL** database language at IBM San Jose in the 1970s, they lifted PL/I's `CHAR VARYING` directly into SQL—giving the world **`VARCHAR`**, the most common text column type in every database on Earth!

Likewise, PL/I's hardware-backed exact `DECIMAL(p, q)` data type became SQL's `DECIMAL(p, q)` and inspired the native `decimal` financial type in Microsoft's **C#** and Python's `decimal` module.

questions.prompt: Which ubiquitous SQL database data type is a direct renaming of PL/I's pioneering 'CHARACTER(n) VARYING' string type?
choices: `VARCHAR`, which stores variable-length text up to a maximum length using an internal length prefix.
`BLOB`, which stores unformatted binary photographs on magnetic tape reels.
`FLOAT`, which stores approximate scientific numbers in base-16 hexadecimal notation.
`BOOLEAN`, which stores a single 1-bit flag inside an 80-column punch card image.
questions.explanation: SQL's `CHARACTER VARYING` (universally abbreviated `VARCHAR`) was modeled directly on PL/I's `CHAR(n) VARYING` length-prefixed string design.

questions.prompt: Beyond variable-length strings, what other core PL/I data representation was adopted directly into SQL and modern enterprise languages like C#?
choices: Implicit I–N variable typing based on the first letter of a database column name.
Exact fixed-point `DECIMAL(p, q)` arithmetic for rounding-free financial and currency calculations.
Hollerith overpunch zones that store negative signs as holes in the top edge of a disk sector.
Self-modifying `ALTER` goto statements that rewrite database queries at runtime.
questions.explanation: PL/I's exact `DECIMAL(p, q)` data type (total digits `p`, fractional digits `q`) was carried straight into SQL's `DECIMAL`/`NUMERIC` types and inspired C#'s native `decimal` type.

chunks.title: PL/I's Fingerprints Across C, Ada, Java, and Python
chunks.content_markdown:
Once you learn to spot **PL/I architectural DNA**, you begin to see its fingerprints across almost every modern programming tool. Whenever a programmer in C, C++, Java, C#, JavaScript, CSS, SQL, or Rust wraps a note inside `/* ... */` block comments, they are typing punctuation invented for PL/I in 1964 after free-form code made punch-card comment columns obsolete. Likewise, PL/I's explicit `POINTER` variables and `ALLOCATE` / `FREE` commands brought dynamic heap memory into mainstream high-level languages, directly shaping Pascal, C, and C++.

Even modern error recovery and data science trace key roots back to PL/I. Its pioneering `ON`-conditions (`ON ZERODIVIDE`, `ON ENDFILE`) proved that a high-level program could intercept runtime faults and recover gracefully—a breakthrough refined by **Ada**, **C++**, **Java**, **Python**, and **C#** into structured `try / catch` exception blocks. And PL/I's whole-array expressions (`A = B * 2;`) and asterisk cross-section slicing (`A(*, 3)`) directly anticipated the vector and matrix slicing at the heart of **MATLAB**, **Julia**, **R**, and Python's **NumPy**.

questions.prompt: How did PL/I's pioneering `ON`-condition error-handling mechanism influence modern languages like Ada, C++, Java, Python, and C#?
choices: It inspired structured `try / catch` exception handling so programs can intercept and recover from runtime errors.
It convinced modern language designers that all runtime arithmetic faults should immediately halt the operating system.
It established the IEEE rule that division by zero must return zero silently without raising any signal.
It required compilers to repair runtime divide-by-zero errors by substituting random positive integers.
questions.explanation: PL/I was the first mainstream language to provide programmable runtime condition handling (`ON ZERODIVIDE`, etc.), which later languages refined into lexical `try / catch` exception blocks.

questions.prompt: Which modern data-science feature in Python's NumPy, MATLAB, and Julia was already present in 1964 PL/I?
choices: Automatic backpropagation of gradients across graphics processing unit clusters.
Interactive notebook cells rendered inside a graphical web browser window.
Whole-array arithmetic expressions and cross-section slicing of rows and columns.
Built-in parsing of comma-separated spreadsheet files directly from cloud storage.
questions.explanation: PL/I supported whole-array operations (`A = B + C;`) and asterisk cross-section slicing (`A(*, 3)`), decades before array-oriented scientific tools like MATLAB and NumPy popularized them.

chunks.title: Epilogue: The Cathedral That Quarry-Built the Modern World
chunks.content_markdown:
In medieval history, builders sometimes raised a cathedral so vast and ambitious that its towering spires could never quite be finished as planned—yet over the centuries, townspeople used the finely cut stones from its quarry to build every bridge, schoolhouse, and guildhall across the valley.

**PL/I** is computing history's great cathedral. Conceived in 1964 to unify the fractured worlds of scientific FORTRAN, commercial COBOL, and low-level assembly on the IBM System/360, it stumbled over the 64-kilobyte Hursley compiler squeeze, its own "Swiss Army knife" complexity, and its overly permissive conversion and division rules. It never became the one final language that replaced all others.

Yet in daring to assemble block structure, recursion, pointers, variable-length strings, exact decimals, array slicing, multitasking, and exception handling under one roof sixty years ago, PL/I proved what high-level languages could achieve—and quietly supplied the building blocks of the modern software world.

questions.prompt: Why does the metaphor of an ambitious cathedral whose stones built the surrounding town fit PL/I's place in computing history?
choices: PL/I compilers were originally funded and maintained by European cathedral preservation societies.
PL/I source decks were archived on engraved metal plates after magnetic tape was retired in 1980.
Although full PL/I never replaced all rivals, its pioneering features were absorbed into almost every modern language.
IBM dismantled its unsold System/360 mainframes and recycled their components into personal computers.
questions.explanation: While PL/I failed to replace all other languages as a single monolith, its innovations—from `VARCHAR` and `DECIMAL` to `/* */` comments, pointers, array slicing, and exception handling—built the modern programming landscape.

questions.prompt: Looking back across both parts of our PL/I journey, what dual lesson does PL/I's history teach software engineers today?
choices: Bold language innovation advances computing, but unchecked complexity and silent implicit rules carry steep costs.
Programming languages should never combine text strings and decimal numbers inside the same compiler.
Hand-written assembly language is always more portable and maintainable than structured high-level code.
A compiler's memory footprint and speed have very little influence on real-world developer adoption.
questions.explanation: PL/I's story celebrates extraordinary technical foresight while reminding designers that simplicity, transparent performance, and strict compile-time safety nets are essential for human programmers.
